new_prompt:
Design a 3:4 vertical poster split into a 3x3 grid that can be sliced into nine separate carousel images.

Inputs
- Theme: [e.g. better sleep tips]
- Audience: [e.g. busy young professionals]
- Brand colours: [default: cream white, beige, light caramel, dark brown text]

Layout
- Tile 1: cover with a bold title (max 6 words) and a one-line hook.
- Tiles 2-9: one tip each, with a heading (max 5 words), one or two plain sentences, and a small flat illustration of [an object that matches the tip].

new_title: Turn Facts Into a Dramatic Monologue
new_prompt:
Recast the passage below as a stage monologue without losing a single fact.

Inputs
- Passage: [paste]
- Speaker: [who is talking, e.g. a museum curator on the night the exhibit closes]
- Audience on stage: [who they address]
- Length: [e.g. 250-350 words, about 2 minutes spoken]

Requirements
- Every fact in the passage appears, accurately; add emotion, rhythm and imagery, never new facts or dates.
- Open with a line that grabs attention, build to a turning point, and end on a strong closing line.
- Include 2-3 bracketed stage directions, e.g. [pauses].

After the monologue, list each fact from the passage and the line where it appears, so I can check nothing was dropped.

new_title: Bullet Summary of a Big Idea
new_prompt:
Explain [philosophy, movement or theory, e.g. Stoicism] to a curious beginner.

Output
1. One-sentence definition.
2. Up to 10 bullets, one idea each, in plain words (no jargon unless you define it), ordered: core belief → key concepts → famous figures or texts → common misunderstandings → how people practise it today.
3. 'Try this' box: one small exercise a reader could do this week.
4. Two reputable starting points for further reading, with author and title. Don't invent sources; if unsure, say so.

Keep the whole answer under [250] words and stay neutral; present it, don't advocate for it.

new_title: Light Limerick on a Chosen Subject
new_prompt:
Write a playful limerick about [subject, e.g. a cat who believes it owns the neighbourhood].

Rules
- Five lines, AABBA rhyme.
- Lines 1, 2 and 5 have three stressed beats; lines 3 and 4 have two.
- Clean, family-friendly humour, with a twist in the last line.
- Use [one detail to include, e.g. the cat's name, Biscuit].

Output: the limerick, then a second alternative, then one line naming the twist in each. Read each aloud in your head and fix any line where the rhythm stumbles.

Write a short fish-out-of-water story.

Inputs
- Character: [name and one trait]
- Their world, where they excel: [e.g. alpine skiing]
- Unfamiliar situation: [e.g. a night shift at a busy diner]
- Tone: [funny or warm]
- Length: under 300 words

Requirements
- Show their expertise in the opening lines, then drop them into the new situation.
- Three escalating mistakes, each caused by applying their old skills wrongly.
- A turning point where one old skill unexpectedly helps.
- An ending that shows what they learned.

Give it a title.

new_title: Techniques to Remember What I Read
new_prompt:
I forget most of what I read in [kind of material, e.g. business books]. Give me memory techniques I can start tonight.

About me: [reading time per week, format: paper / e-reader / audio]

Output (under 200 words)
- 5 techniques as a numbered list. For each: name, how to do it in one sentence, and when to use it (during / right after / a week later).
- A 10-minute weekly review routine that combines them.
- One-line explanation of why spaced review works.

Prefer methods with good evidence (retrieval practice, spacing, summarising in your own words) over gimmicks.

new_title: Three Quick Fixes for an Everyday Problem
new_prompt:
Help me solve a small everyday problem with three practical options.

Inputs
- Problem: [describe it in a sentence or two]
- Constraints: [budget, time, tools I have, living situation]

Output: three numbered options, cheapest or easiest first. For each:
- What to do (1-3 steps)
- Rough time and cost (mark costs 'approx.')
- One thing to watch out for
- How I'll know it worked

No preamble. If the problem could signal a safety issue (electrical, gas, health), say so first and recommend a professional.
